uncited: The architecture consists of a Sky Encoder and a Sky Decoder (2D UNet).
The decoder reconstructs the HDR sky from the encoded features.
**Peak Direction Encoding:** A 1-channel tensor $E_{dir} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times H \times W}$.
**Peak Intensity Encoding:** A 3-channel tensor $E_{int} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}$.
*   **End-to-end training:** Updating the encoder and the rest of the network.

To edit the sky, the user modifies the explicit components of the sky vector $\hat{f}$ to create an edited vector $\hat{f}^{edit} = (\hat{f}_{intensity}^{edit}, \hat{f}_{dir}^{edit}, \hat{f}_{latent})$.
*   **Time Complexity:** The encoder uses a ResNet50 backbone followed by lightweight CNN branches, making feature extraction comparable to standard ResNet50 inference.
The decoder is a 2D UNet, which is computationally efficient for image-to-image translation.
*   **Memory Complexity:** The sky feature vector is small ($\mathbb{R}^{64}$), allowing for efficient transmission and storage compared to full HDR environment maps.
The decoder requires memory proportional to the image resolution ($64 \times 256$).
*   Relies on the quality of the LDR input; artifacts in the LDR panorama may propagate to the HDR output.
*   **When not to use:** If the scene has no dominant light source or if the sky is uniformly overcast, the explicit peak model may introduce artifacts.
The work addresses the challenge of estimating HDR lighting for street scenes to enable realistic virtual object insertion.
A key component is the sky modeling network, which learns a low-dimensional feature space for the sky dome.
